note.note:
History:
- Main complaint: Recurrent frontal headaches affecting work; additional intermittent symptoms include palpitations, shortness of breath while seated at desk, tingling in both hands, reduced appetite, ~5 lb unintentional weight loss, and decreased libido.
- Onset/duration/progression: Began around time of changing jobs; ongoing. Symptoms occur mostly at work and at different times (not all together).
- Context/triggers: Lawyer in London; workload ~50% meetings and 50% computer work; stress rated 7–8/10. Headaches occur during meetings or while on laptop. Palpitations sometimes triggered when entering the elevator in the morning; occur ~once daily or more. Shortness of breath occurs while sitting at desk; not with exercise. Commute does not trigger headaches.
- Associated symptoms: Headaches sometimes with mild nausea. Tingling described in both hands (no leg tingling).
- Relevant negatives: No prior history of similar headaches before current episodes. No shortness of breath with exercise.
- “Feeling hot”: Initially listed in intake note, but patient did not clearly endorse; instead described intermittent shortness of breath (conflict noted).

Past Medical History:
- Thyroid disease: Patient states “hyperthyroidism,” but is taking thyroxine (levothyroxine) — potential inconsistency; needs clarification (conflict noted).
- Other conditions: None reported.
- Medications: Levothyroxine (thyroxine) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Allergies: No known drug allergies reported.
- Social: Alcohol ~once weekly (a couple of glasses of wine). Non-smoker. No recreational drug use.

Physical Examination:
- Not recorded (tele-visit; no vitals or in-person exam documented).

Impression:
- Likely work-related stress/anxiety with tension-type headaches and somatic symptoms; rule out thyroid dysfunction contributing to palpitations and weight loss.
- Top differentials (consistent with transcript):
  - Work-related anxiety/panic with hyperventilation: Onset with job change; symptoms cluster at work; elevator triggers palpitations; dyspnea at rest but not with exertion; bilateral hand tingling.
  - Thyroid dysfunction (possible over-replacement): On thyroxine with palpitations, mild unintentional weight loss, decreased libido; “feeling hot” not clearly endorsed.
  - Tension-type headache: Frontal headache during meetings/computer use; high occupational stress; mild nausea; no focal neurologic deficits reported.
- Conflicts: Intake note “feeling hot” not confirmed by patient; thyroid history vs medication suggests possible mislabeling (hyperthyroid vs hypothyroid on replacement) — conflict noted.

Management Plan:
- In-person evaluation: Schedule clinic appointment via app for focused cardiovascular and respiratory exam; assess blood pressure and perform neurologic screening.
- Labs: Thyroid function blood tests (per plan discussed). Clarify thyroid diagnosis and levothyroxine dosing.
- No medications started pending in-person assessment and labs.
- At visit, consider:
  - Standardized anxiety/depression screening (e.g., GAD-7/PHQ-9) given work stress and symptom pattern.
  - Ergonomic review and structured screen breaks; maintain regular meals and hydration to help headaches and appetite.
- Safety-net: Seek urgent care if severe/worsening chest pain, syncope, new focal neurologic deficits, or a sudden “worst” headache occur.

Patient Summary:
- 35-year-old lawyer with new-onset, work-associated frontal headaches plus intermittent palpitations, dyspnea at rest, bilateral hand tingling, reduced appetite, mild unintentional weight loss, and decreased libido since changing jobs. Pattern and triggers suggest stress/anxiety with tension-type headache; thyroid dysfunction remains a consideration. Plan is in-person exam and thyroid testing before starting any treatment.

Key Takeaways:
- Book and attend the in-person clinic appointment for examination and thyroid blood tests.
- No new medications will be started until evaluation is complete.
- Track symptom timing/triggers (meetings, screen time, elevator) to review at the visit.

Next Steps:
- Schedule clinic visit via app.
- Complete thyroid function tests at or prior to the visit.
- Based on exam/labs, consider additional tests if indicated (e.g., CBC, B12/ferritin) and discuss stress management options and ergonomics.

Quality checks:
- Missing elements: Vitals (including BP, HR), full neurologic exam, thyroid-focused exam, oxygen saturation, detailed headache characterization (duration, quality, photophobia/phonophobia, aura), sleep/caffeine history, comprehensive medication list with doses, family history, and confirmed allergy status.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx/record: Intake note reports “feeling hot,” patient did not affirm this; patient states “hyperthyroidism” but is on levothyroxine (possible hypothyroidism on replacement) — conflict noted.
- Transcript quality: Generally clear; some hesitations/overlaps but clinical content understandable.
